questions.stem: Phillip, 60, a hypertensive smoker, has 40 minutes of ongoing central chest pressure. You are doing a focused cardiovascular examination in the GP clinic before he is given aspirin. Which examination step best screens for acute aortic dissection?
options: Auscultate for a third heart sound at the apex in the left lateral position
Assess the height of the JVP with the patient reclining at 45 degrees
Measure the blood pressure in both arms and compare the two readings
Palpate the apex beat for its position and character
questions.why: Before antithrombotic treatment, compare the blood pressure in both arms. A difference of more than 20 mmHg suggests dissection. Also check for pulse deficits, radio-femoral delay and an early diastolic aortic regurgitation murmur. Phillip's arm pressures were equal (150/90 and 146/88 mmHg).
notes: A third heart sound points to left ventricular failure or volume overload, not dissection.
The JVP shows right heart filling pressure and fluid status; it does not help you pick up a dissection.
The apex beat shows left ventricular hypertrophy or dilatation from long-standing hypertension; it does not tell you about the aorta.

questions.stem: Phillip, 60, has an anterior STEMI on the GP clinic ECG and you have called 000. He has ongoing pain at 7/10, BP 144/88 mmHg and SpO2 95% on room air. He has no allergies, no bleeding history and takes only ramipril and atorvastatin. Which treatment should you give now while waiting for the ambulance?
options: Aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed or dissolved
Oxygen 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask
Morphine 10 mg intramuscularly into the deltoid
Metoprolol 50 mg orally to slow the heart rate
questions.why: Give aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed, as soon as possible to anyone with suspected STEMI unless they are allergic or actively bleeding. It irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 and reduces mortality.
notes: Oxygen is only for hypoxaemia (SpO2 below 93%), titrated to 93 to 96%. Routine oxygen at SpO2 95% has no benefit.
Avoid IM injections because he may need fibrinolysis, which can cause a haematoma. IM absorption is also unreliable. Give titrated IV opioid instead.
Beta-blockers are not started in general practice before transfer. An early beta-blocker in an evolving anterior STEMI can bring on cardiogenic shock.

questions.stem: Phillip, 60, with an evolving anterior STEMI, is given sublingual GTN 400 micrograms in the GP clinic. His pain eases slightly for a minute and then returns, and he develops a mild headache. What is the main mechanism by which GTN relieves ischaemic chest pain?
options: Dilates the occluded left anterior descending artery to restore flow
Blocks L-type calcium channels, reducing myocardial contractility
Dilates systemic arterioles, mainly lowering afterload at usual doses
Raises cGMP in venous smooth muscle, cutting preload and wall stress
questions.why: GTN releases nitric oxide, which activates guanylate cyclase and raises cGMP. The main effect is venodilation, which lowers preload, LV wall tension and myocardial oxygen demand. It cannot open a thrombotic occlusion, so the relief is only brief.
notes: An artery blocked by thrombus does not open with vasodilation. That is why his pain comes back and he needs reperfusion.
Blocking calcium channels is how verapamil and diltiazem work; GTN acts through nitric oxide and cGMP.
At usual sublingual doses GTN mainly dilates the veins. Its effect on the arterioles and afterload is small.

questions.stem: Phillip, 60, has ongoing chest pain. His ECG shows new ST elevation in V1 to V4 (3 mm in V2 and V3), 0.5 mm ST elevation in aVL and reciprocal ST depression in II, III and aVF. Where is the coronary occlusion most likely to be?
options: Right coronary artery, proximal to the acute marginal branch
Left anterior descending artery, proximal to the first diagonal branch
Left circumflex artery, proximal to the first obtuse marginal branch
Left anterior descending artery, distal to the first diagonal branch
questions.why: V1 to V4 is the LAD territory. ST elevation in aVL means the high lateral wall, supplied by the first diagonal branch, is also involved. Together with inferior reciprocal depression, this points to a proximal LAD occlusion before the first diagonal, which puts a large area of myocardium at risk.
notes: An RCA occlusion causes ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Here those leads show depression.
A circumflex occlusion affects the lateral or posterior leads (I, aVL, V5, V6, or ST depression in V1 to V3), not elevation from V1 to V4.
An occlusion beyond the first diagonal spares the high lateral wall, so you would not expect ST elevation in aVL with reciprocal inferior depression.
